experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Split.** The paper presents itself as one experiment but studies two classes with disjoint samples, different exams and different graders, so it is coded as two experiments under the PROMPT.md rule "a new task or a new sample is a new experiment". This element is the Introduction to American Law and Legal Reasoning class (undergraduates, n = 32 of 128 enrolled, roughly 23%).

**Arms.** One human-AI arm ("AI-Assisted", students taking the exam with GPT-4 access through the authors' ChatGPT clone site). Human-alone reference = the same 32 students' real spring-2023 exam, on which GPT-4 was banned (within-subjects). AI-alone reference = four AI-only exams, one per prompting method (basic, chain-of-thought, few-shot, grounded); those four are reference runs, not conditions, because the prompting manipulation was never applied to the assisted students.

**Percentile scale caveat (important).** All values are percentile points, but the reference cohorts differ: the "Human-Only Mean" row ranks the volunteers' real 2023 scores against all students enrolled in the 2023 class, whereas the "AI-Assisted Mean" row and Table 2's GPT-4 values rank against the students who sat the same exam in 2022 (PDF p.15, p.19).

**AI-alone values: one row per prompting method.** Table 2 (p.20) prints four AI-only exams per component, one per prompting method (basic, chain-of-thought, few-shot, grounded), each a single deterministic run at temperature 0. These are four AI configurations, not repeated runs of one system, so they are NOT averaged: every score metric has four measure rows that share the human-alone and AI-assisted values and differ only in the AI-alone value (N_AI = 1, Sd_Perf_AI = 0). The basic prompt is the paper's default and the closest to the participants' free-form use; the grounded prompt (100 MC / 93 essay) is the basis for the paper's claim that "GPT-4 alone outperformed both humans and AI-assisted humans on average". Analyses that need one AI-alone value per component should pick one row (basic as the primary, the others as sensitivity).

**Task_Type.** Coded Decide. The multiple-choice half is graded mechanically against a key; the essay half is graded against a detailed instructor rubric that "assigned specific points for different elements of the exam answer" (PDF p.30), which PROMPT.md puts under Decide ("structured ... legal reasoning", "scored against ... an expert rubric"). A coder who treats issue-spotter essay writing as open-ended production would code Create; the essay measure row is the one affected.

**Task_Output** is mixed within one exam: multiple-choice selections (Categoric) plus a written essay (Text). Recorded as the free-text value "Categoric and Text".

**Interaction_Mode.** free_use: participants had an unrestricted ChatGPT-style chat window during the exam. The multiple-choice training protocol (PDF p.10 fn.43) asked them to draft their own answer while GPT-4 generated one and then reconcile, which has a human_first flavour, but no arm restricted how the tool could be used.

**Letter grades (not coded as measure rows, since the fields are numeric).** PDF p.22: median grade without AI = B; with AI = A-. GPT-4 alone = A- (basic), B+ (chain-of-thought), A (few-shot), A (grounded), against a whole-class median of B+.

**Exclusions / sample caveats.** 39 students signed up, 32 completed (PDF p.10 fn.42). The authors note the volunteer sample under-represents both low and high performers (PDF p.30), and that Figure 4's heterogeneity result may partly reflect mean reversion (PDF p.18). An essay grading correction factor of -1.42 points out of 53 was applied for year-over-year grader drift (PDF p.13); the 2022/2023 regrading correlation was 0.77 (Spearman).

**N_Exp.** The participant count is footnote 42 (PDF p.10): thirty-two completed the Introduction to American Law study, sixteen the Insurance Law study; the number is spelled out in words, so a verbatim number search will not find it.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Split.** This element is the Insurance Law class: a separate sample of 16 of 52 enrolled students (roughly 31%), a separate exam (two complex issue-spotter essay questions, no multiple choice), graded by the instructor rather than by research assistants. See the split rationale in the Introduction to American Law element.

**Arms.** One human-AI arm ("AI-Assisted"). Human-alone reference = the same 16 students' real spring-2023 exam without AI (within-subjects). AI-alone reference = four AI-only exams, one per prompting method; reference runs, not conditions.

**Percentile scale caveat.** Same as the other experiment: the human-alone percentile is ranked against the 2023 class, the AI-assisted and AI-alone percentiles against the 2022 cohort (PDF p.15, p.19).

**AI-alone values: one row per prompting method** (5 / 15 / 30 / 65 for basic / chain-of-thought / few-shot / grounded, Table 2 p.20), each a single deterministic run at temperature 0, so N_AI = 1 and Sd_Perf_AI = 0 and no averaging across configurations. The spread is very large, from bottom-of-class with the basic prompt to moderately above average when grounded; the basic prompt is the primary comparator (paper's default, closest to participants' free-form use).

**Missing reference arm.** The Time row has no human-alone value: "We were not able to track how long study participants took to complete their actual final exam in Insurance Law" (PDF p.22). The percentile row is complete for all three arms.

**Participants.** "upper-level 2L and 3L University of Minnesota Law students" (PDF p.10); one participant was an undergraduate, and the paper states results are unchanged when that person is excluded (PDF p.10 fn.41). Participant_Type_2 coded "Students"; a coder following the "professionals in training" reading of the codebook could instead use "Specialists (Non-Expert)". Participant_Expert coded false: they are law students, not practising insurance lawyers, although they had just completed the course.

**Task scope.** Participants answered two of the three questions from the real spring 2022 final, i.e. half of the real exam, each question having counted for 25% of the 2022 course grade (PDF p.29).

**Task_Type.** Coded Decide (structured legal reasoning scored against an instructor rubric); Create is the defensible alternative for open-ended issue-spotter essays.

**Letter grades (not coded as measure rows).** PDF p.22: median grade without AI = B/B+, and with AI assistance "that median grade was unchanged". GPT-4 alone = B (basic), B/B+ (chain-of-thought), B+ (few-shot), A- (grounded), against a whole-class median of B+.

**Grading.** An essay correction factor of +1.375 points out of 50 was applied for year-over-year grader drift; the 2022/2023 regrading correlation was 0.94 (Spearman) because the same professor graded both years (PDF p.13).

**N_Exp.** The participant count is footnote 42 (PDF p.10): thirty-two completed the Introduction to American Law study, sixteen the Insurance Law study; the number is spelled out in words, so a verbatim number search will not find it.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
Single prospective, randomized, single-blind (to the rater) trial with one human-AI arm and two reference arms.

- **Arms.** Human-AI condition = physicians randomized to GPT-4 via ChatGPT Plus *in addition to* conventional resources. Human-alone reference arm = physicians randomized to conventional resources only (explicitly instructed not to use any LLM). AI-alone reference arm = "GPT Alone": the study team copy-pasted the five cases and questions into a zero-shot prompt and ran each prompt five times (5 cases x 5 runs = 25 observations), graded blind alongside the human responses.
- **Participants.** 92 practicing attending and resident physicians in internal medicine, family medicine or emergency medicine, recruited by email lists from Stanford University, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and the University of Virginia; randomized 46/46 (Figure 1, PDF p. 12). 73% attendings, 27% residents; mean 7.6 years in medical training (Table 1). Residents were paid $100, attendings $200.
- **Ns in the measure rows are participants and runs.** N_Human = N_HumanAI = 46 physicians per arm; N_AI = 5 runs per case. The means and SDs in Table 2 are over cases (178 LLM-arm cases, 197 conventional-arm cases; 25 LLM-alone observations) because "All analyses were at the case level, clustered by the participant" (Methods, PDF p. 9).
- **Discrepancy in case counts.** The Results text (PDF p. 4) states "400 cases were scored in total, 176 from the group of physicians using the LLM, 199 from physicians using only conventional resources, and 25 from the LLM alone", whereas Table 2 and the legends of Figures 2-4 report 178 LLM cases and 197 conventional cases (375 total, plus 25 LLM-alone). Both add to 375 physician cases. The table values (178/197) were used, per protocol.
- **AI-alone data are limited.** The GPT-4-alone arm has a total-score mean only (43.7%, Results p. 4 and Figure 3). No SD is printed for it anywhere and Figure 3 is a boxplot with no printed numbers, so Sd_Perf_AI is left null rather than estimated. No domain sub-scores and no timing were reported for the GPT-alone arm.
- **Sign of the LLM-alone contrast.** Results (p. 4): LLM alone vs physicians with LLM = 0.9% (95% CI -7.2 to 9.0, p = 0.80). Abstract (p. 2): "-0.9%, 95% CI -9.0 to 7.2, p=0.8". Same comparison reported in opposite directions; neither changes a mean used here.
- **Rubric domain sub-scores are NOT coded as measure rows** because the LLM-alone arm is not reported for them (protocol rule for sub-scores). For reference, Physicians+LLM vs Physicians+Conventional in Table 2: Management 40.5 (19.1) vs 33.4 (17.3), n = 178/197, difference 6.1 (2.5 to 9.7), p = 0.001; Factual 62.9 (37.6) vs 53.8 (39.6), n = 69/78, difference 9.6 (-3.1 to 22.3), p = 0.14; Diagnostic 56.8 (37.6) vs 45.8 (26.7), n = 72/77, difference 12.1 (3.1 to 21.0), p = 0.009; Specific 42.4 (20.2) vs 34.9 (17.9), n = 178/197, difference 6.2 (2.4 to 9.9), p = 0.002; General 29.4 (15.0) vs 26.5 (13.0), n = 70/80, difference 3.3 (-1.3 to 7.9), p = 0.2.
- **Exploratory harm analysis not coded as a measure row** (response level, no Ns, no SDs, no AI-alone comparator; Supplement 5 is not bundled in this PDF). Text on PDF p. 5: medium and high likelihood of harm in 8.3% and 3.8% of LLM-assisted responses vs 11.4% and 2.9% of conventional responses; mild-to-moderate harm 3.7% vs 5.3%; severe harm 7.6% vs 7.5%.
- **Task type.** Answers are free text (Task_Output = Text) but are scored against expert-developed Delphi rubrics, so Task_Type is coded Decide under the protocol rule ("scored against a reference answer or an expert rubric ... structured clinical reasoning"). A coder who weights the open-ended production would read it as Create; this is the single most debatable code in this record.
- **Not in this PDF.** Supplements 1-5 and Extended Display Items 1-4 are referenced but not bundled (pdfdetach: 0 embedded files), so the zero-shot prompt, the harm tables and the ANOVA sensitivity analysis could not be inspected.
- Only potentially correct answers were given credit; wrong answers were not penalized. Pilot studies and two 10-person rubric-validation datasets were excluded from the analysis.

paper_metadata.title: AI Agents for Inventory Control: Human-LLM-OR Complementarity

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**What is and is not recorded here.** The paper has two parts. *Part 1* (Section 4, "Algorithmic Experiment") is a purely algorithmic benchmark: 1,320 InventoryBench instances x four methods (OR, LLM, OR->LLM, LLM->OR) x three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, GPT-5 Mini), with **no human participants**, hence no human-alone arm and no human-AI arm. It is therefore not recorded as a separate experiment; its headline numbers are Table 1a (Gemini 3 Flash, 1,320 instances): OR 0.445 +/-0.018, LLM 0.494 +/-0.018, OR->LLM 0.538 +/-0.016, LLM->OR 0.501 +/-0.018. *Part 2* (Section 5) is the classroom human-in-the-loop experiment recorded here.

**Arms and how they map to conditions.** Table 1b (p. 3) reports five arms on the same three real-data instances: three human collaboration modes and two algorithm-only benchmarks.
- Mode A (OR->Human), 0.466 +/-0.025 -> the HUMAN-ALONE reference arm (the paper's own mapping, footnote 8 p. 18 and Section 6.2: Human-only = Mode A, AI-only = OR->LLM, Human-AI team = Mode B). Participants always saw at least the OR recommendation, so no unaided-human arm exists; the OR pipeline is a capped base-stock heuristic (Xin 2021; Appendix A), an algorithm the paper never calls AI. Mode A is therefore NOT coded as a human–AI condition.
- Mode B (OR->LLM->Human), 0.534 +/-0.020 -> `conditions[0]`
- Mode C (OR->LLM + Guidance), 0.464 +/-0.018 -> `conditions[1]`
- OR (no human), 0.376, no CI (deterministic, 1 run per instance) -> algorithm-only benchmark for Mode A; not used in a measure row
- OR->LLM (no human), 0.482 +/-0.007 (100 runs per instance) -> AI-alone reference for Modes B and C

**Reference arms.** `Avg_Perf_Human` = 0.466 (Mode A) is shared by both conditions; `Avg_Perf_AI` = 0.482 (OR->LLM, no human) likewise. The human-alone arm is itself OR-assisted, which is the paper's own analytic choice.

**Coding of the OR aid.** The OR pipeline behind Mode A is a data-driven capped base-stock policy (Xin 2021; Appendix A): it estimates demand mean and SD from history and plugs them into a normal-quantile base-stock formula with a cap. It is an algorithm, not a learned model, and the paper never calls it "AI". An earlier version of this record coded Mode A as a `Shallow`-AI condition with a null human-alone arm; that entry was removed on review (it is the human baseline).

**Model used in the human experiment.** Never named inside Section 5. `LLM_Model` = "Gemini 3 Flash" is inferred from p. 9 ("All results in the main body are reported for Gemini 3 Flash") together with p. 14 ("the LLM recommendation (from the same OR->LLM pipeline as Part 1)").

**Participants.** "69 participants" and "187 subject-instance observations in total" (p. 14); some participants did not complete every instance (footnote 4). Per-mode counts are never reported. Recruitment channel, institution, demographics, incentives and prior expertise are not stated; the only descriptors are "classroom experiment", "human participants", and "The game was voluntary with no identification saved or grade impact" (p. 14), which is why `Participant_Source` is null and `Participant_Type_2` = Students is an inference. Hypotheses were pre-registered (https://aspredicted.org/gs5tm3.pdf).

**Design.** Each participant plays all three instances with one mode randomly assigned per instance "so that each participant experiences each mode exactly once" (p. 14); the mode comparison is a pooled OLS with subject and instance fixed effects, SEs clustered by subject (p. 15). Hence Within-Subjects / Dependent Samples for the human vs. human-AI contrast. The human-vs-automated comparisons (Mode A vs OR, Mode B vs OR->LLM) instead pool human observations with algorithm runs, clustering humans by subject and automated observations by run (Appendix J, p. 42).

**Task.** Multi-period inventory control (T = 47 weekly periods for the real H&M instances). Instance 1 = swimwear bottom, lead time 0; Instance 2 = blazer, lead time 1; Instance 3 = trousers, stochastic lead time (1 with probability 75%, infinite otherwise, i.e. lost orders) (Appendix I, p. 42). Participants see a product image and text description, on-hand and in-transit inventory, cumulative reward, p, h, promised lead time, the most recent demand, and historical demand / inventory charts (Figures 6, 12, 13).

**Statistics reported but NOT entered as measure rows** (they are contrasts or derived quantities, not arm means on the metric):
- Mode B > Mode A: tau_B = 0.0675 (SE 0.0185, one-sided p = 0.00025); Mode C - Mode B = -0.0722 (SE 0.0177, two-sided p = 0.00012) (p. 15).
- Mode A > OR: one-sided p = 0.0098; Mode B > OR->LLM: one-sided p = 0.000009 (p. 16).
- Population-level complementarity CE = 0.0496 (one-sided bootstrap p = 0.00010), 10.2% relative gain (p. 18); average individual-level complementarity E_i[CE_i] = 0.0192 (one-sided p = 0.0643); distribution-free lower bound on the fraction with strictly positive complementarity = 0.203 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.147-0.329) (p. 19).

**Eligibility note for the coder.** All three arms (human-alone proxy, AI-alone, human-AI) are present on the same task and the same metric for both conditions, and the task is Decide, so both are eligible. The caveat is that the "human-alone" arm is itself OR-assisted, which is the paper's own analytic choice.

paper_metadata.title: From tool to teammate in a randomized controlled trial of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**One experiment.** A single randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06911645; Stanford IRB 71319), one participant sample and one task, with two clinician-AI workflow arms. The two arms are coded as the two human-AI *conditions*, not as separate experiments.

**Conditions.** (1) *AI as first opinion* - the AI analyses the case and the clinician sees that output before writing their own answer (108 cases, 27 participants). (2) *AI as second opinion* - the clinician answers first using conventional resources, then pastes the vignette plus their own answers into the system and may revise (146 cases, 43 participants). In both arms the system then shows an integrated synthesis of the clinician's and the AI's inferences, highlighting agreements and disagreements, and invites free-form dialogue before the clinician submits final answers.

**Reference arms (both shared across the two conditions).**
- *Human alone (conventional resources, 75%)*: not a separate group. It is the set of **initial, pre-AI responses of the 43 clinicians in the AI-as-second-opinion arm** (146 cases), scored separately (Methods, "Baselines for clinicians and AI", p. 13). Conventional resources were UpToDate, PubMed or Google.
- *AI alone (87%)*: the AI's initial responses drawn from the AI-as-first-opinion arm - five responses randomly selected for each of the six vignettes, yielding 30 scored cases. The paper explicitly reports non-determinism (different outputs for the same vignette across participants), so Sd_Perf_AI is left null rather than set to 0; no SD across the 30 runs is reported.

**Design coding.** Because the human-alone baseline lives inside the AI-as-second-opinion arm, the human vs. human-AI contrast is *within-subjects / dependent samples* for the AI-as-second-opinion condition (same 43 people; N_Human = N_HumanAI = 43) but *between-subjects / independent samples* for the AI-as-first-opinion condition (its 27 clinicians never produced a conventional-resources answer). Exp_Design is coded "Mixed, Within-Subjects" and Comp_Type "Dependent Samples", following the larger arm and the arm that generates the baseline; a coder treating the AI-as-first-opinion condition on its own should read that contrast as Between-Subjects / Independent Samples.

**Numbers that could not become measure rows.**
- *Clinically actionable-decisions sub-score* (final diagnosis + next steps) and *evidence sub-score* (supporting/opposing evidence) are reported only as between-arm mean **differences** (+14.9% for AI-as-second-opinion vs. conventional resources, p=0.00092, 95% CI 6.0%-23%; +8.9% for AI-as-first- vs. AI-as-second-opinion, p=0.026, 95% CI 1.1%-16%; +0.37% evidence sub-score, p=0.74). No arm means are printed and no AI-alone value exists for these sub-scores, so per the protocol rule ("sub-scores are separate rows only when the paper reports all three arms") no rows were created. The Sankey figure (PDF p. 26) gives only case counts per score level for the AI-as-second-opinion arm.
- *Medians*: the Discussion gives a conventional-resources median of 75% and an AI-alone median of 89.5%, but no medians for the two clinician-AI arms, so no median row could be formed.
- The box plot and violin plot (PDF pp. 24-25) print no numeric values on the plotted arms, so nothing was read off them.
- No SD, SE or per-arm CI is reported for any arm mean anywhere in the paper; only CIs of mean differences. All SD fields are therefore null.

**Discrepancies.**
- AI-alone overall score: **87%** (Results, p. 5) vs. **90%** (Abstract, p. 2) vs. **median 89.5%** (Discussion, p. 8). 87% is used because it is the arm mean, on the same scale as the other three values; 90% is most likely a rounding of the 89.5% median.
- The Discussion (p. 8) calls the 75% conventional-resources value a *median* when comparing with the earlier Goh & Gallo study, while the Results and the rest of the Discussion call it a *mean*; the box plot (PDF p. 24) puts the conventional-resources median near 80%, so 75% is treated as the mean.
- In-text figure citations are offset by one from the figure legends (the text cites "Figure 3" for the CONSORT diagram, "Figure 4 / Figure 5" for the score distributions and "Figure 6" for the Sankey, while the legends number them 2, 3/4 and 5). Evidence "page" values are PDF pages, not figure numbers.

**Other.** 71 clinicians took part; 1 was excluded for prior exposure to the vignettes, leaving 70 analysed (39 residents, 31 attendings; 97% internal medicine). 298 cases were captured, 6 removed with the excluded participant and 38 excluded as unfinished, leaving 254 analysed cases. Inter-grader ICC = 0.91. 6 of 70 participants (all AI-as-second-opinion) deviated from the procedure but were retained under intention-to-treat. In 10% of AI-as-second-opinion cases the system failed to display the joint synthesis view. The sample mixes attendings (clearly Specialists (Expert)) with residents (arguably professionals in training); all are U.S.-licensed physicians performing a medical diagnostic task, so Participant_Type_2 is coded "Specialists (Expert)". All supplementary figures and tables cited in the text (Supplementary Figures 1-6, Supplementary Tables 1-2) are NOT bundled in this 29-page PDF, and `pdfdetach -list` reports 0 embedded files; Figure 1 (the synthesis view) is also absent from the rendered pages.

paper_metadata.title: Fusing ChatGPT and Human Decisions in Unfamiliar Face Matching

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Re-analysis of previously collected human data.** Human responses come from Kramer et al. (2021, 2023); 102 participants completed the short version of the Glasgow Face Matching Test (40 trials). Only each participant's first session was used, so the two source samples (n = 52 no interval, n = 50 one-week interval) could be combined.

paper_metadata.title: Benchmarking Human–AI collaboration for common evidence appraisal tools

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**What this experiment is.** Benchmark of five LLMs against human raters on PRISMA appraisal of reporting in 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses in pediatric surgery (27 items x 112 publications = up to 3024 ratings). The human ratings were pre-existing data shared by Cullis and colleagues [14]; the two raters were content experts (British pediatric surgeons).

**Reference arms, shared by all five conditions.** Human-alone = individual human rater 1 (Table 2: 2686/3024 = 89%, 95% CI 87%-90%; kappa 0.81, 95% CI 0.78-0.83). AI-alone = the matching individual LLM in Table 2. Human rater 2's accuracy (90%) is given in the running text only (Section 3.1.1) and ratings from human rater 2 were missing for 15 publications, so rater 2 is not used as the human-alone value.

**Why the human-AI arms are conditions and how they work.** Ratings of individual human rater 1 were combined with individual LLM ratings by a fixed rule: items where the LLM aligned with the human rater were scored against human consensus; inconsistent items were "deferred to a second human rater". The pairing is retrospective and simulated - the human ratings pre-existed and the LLM ratings were produced independently through an API, so neither party saw the other's output. Hence Interaction_Mode = fusion, Final_Decision = AI and Division_Labor = true. Exp_Design is coded Within-Subjects / Dependent Samples because the same human rater 1 ratings underlie both the human-alone and the human-AI value.

**Arms NOT coded as conditions.** Table 3 block (3) "Combined LLMs (consistent in 5/9 ... 9/9)" are LLM-only ensembles of nine LLM assessments with no human involved (PRISMA: accuracy 75%-88% while deferring 4%-74% of ratings). Supplementary Table 2 (not bundled with this PDF) reportedly contains human rater 2 x LLM pairs; only human rater 1 pairs are printed here.

**Scale and denominators.** Accuracy in a human-AI arm is calculated on the nondeferred ratings only, so its denominator is smaller than the human-alone and LLM-alone denominators; all denominators are recorded in the Notes of each measure row. The deferring fraction is the complementary workload measure and has no human-alone or LLM-alone counterpart (both rate every item), so those two values are null in that row.

**N conventions.** N_Exp = 2 human raters. N_Human = N_HumanAI = 1 because the human-alone and human-AI values both come from the single human rater 1; N_AI = 1: one API run per publication at temperature 0 (a duplicate run was made only to measure intrarater reliability); the number of LLM ratings evaluated is recorded in each row's Notes.

**Dispersion.** The paper reports no SDs anywhere; bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples at the publication level) are given instead and are transcribed into each row's Notes. Nothing was computed or estimated (Est_ES = false throughout). Sd_Perf_AI = 0 follows the codebook convention for an AI reported as a single value (all API queries used temperature 0), although duplicate runs were not perfectly reproducible (LLM intrarater reliability 67%-94% for PRISMA).

**Significance.** Human-AI collaboration with Claude-3-Opus, Claude-2, GPT-3.5 and Mixtral-8x22B was significantly more accurate than either human rater alone (8 of 10 possible human-AI pairs across raters 1 and 2); the GPT-4 pairing was not (Table 3, non-bold cells).

**Missing LLM ratings.** Claude-3-Opus could not process 3/112 publications; GPT-4 could not process 3 lengthy publications (for PRISMA and AMSTAR combined); GPT-3.5 could not process 3/112; Mixtral-8x22B could not process 1/112.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**What this experiment is.** Benchmark of five LLMs against human raters on PRECIS-2 appraisal of the pragmatism of 56 randomized controlled trials from the PragMeta database (9 domains x 56 publications = up to 504 ratings), rated ordinally from 1 (very explanatory) to 5 (very pragmatic) or NA. New task and new sample, hence a separate experiment.

**Reference arms, shared by all five conditions.** Human-alone = individual human rater 1 (Table 2: 379/504 = 75%, 95% CI 70%-80%; weighted kappa 0.57, 95% CI 0.48-0.65). AI-alone = the matching individual LLM in Table 2. Human rater 2's accuracy (73%) is given in the running text only (Section 3.1.1).

**Participants / N_Exp caveat.** Human rater 1 was an experienced systematic reviewer and meta-researcher. The role of human rater 2 was filled by one of three people - one of two experienced postgraduate MSc students in epidemiology with special training in PRECIS-2 assessment, or a senior clinical epidemiologist and expert in pragmatic trial design. N_Exp is coded 2 (the number of rater roles analysed per publication, matching "independent ratings from 2 human raters"); the number of distinct individuals could be 4, but the paper never states a total.

**Why the human-AI arms are conditions and how they work.** Same fixed fusion rule as for PRISMA and AMSTAR; neither party saw the other's output. Interaction_Mode = fusion, Final_Decision = AI, Division_Labor = true, Exp_Design = Within-Subjects / Dependent Samples.

**Metric detail.** For the ordinal PRECIS-2 ratings, responses 1 and 2 were pooled to "1/2" and responses 4 and 5 to "4/5", and a weighted version of Cohen's kappa was used; the kappa measure row is therefore weighted kappa, whereas PRISMA and AMSTAR use unweighted Cohen's kappa. Task_Output is coded Numeric (a 1-5 rating); Categoric would also be defensible given the pooling.

**Arms NOT coded as conditions.** Table 3 block (3) "Combined LLMs (consistent in 5/9 ... 9/9)" - LLM-only ensembles, no human (PRECIS-2: accuracy 64%-79% while deferring 29%-88% of ratings).

**Scale, denominators, N conventions and dispersion.** Human-AI accuracy is computed on nondeferred ratings only, and the deferring fractions here are very large (70%-76%), so the human-AI denominators are small (123-149 ratings). Denominators and bootstrap 95% CIs are recorded in each measure row's Notes. N_Human = N_HumanAI = 1 (human rater 1); N_AI = 1 (one run at temperature 0; the number of LLM ratings evaluated is in each row's Notes). No SDs are reported; Sd_Perf_AI = 0 by codebook convention for a single reported AI value at temperature 0.

**Significance.** Only the combination of human rater 2 with GPT-3.5 was significantly more accurate than human rater 2 alone (1 of 10 possible human-AI pairs); none of the human rater 1 pairings printed in Table 3 reached significance against the human rater alone. The authors conclude that human-AI collaboration does not reduce workload for complex tasks such as PRECIS-2.

**Missing LLM ratings.** GPT-3.5 could persistently not process 2 of 56 publications (3.6%) for PRECIS-2; all other models processed all 56.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Scope of this record.** Section 4 of the paper (verifier benchmarking on six text-classification datasets, Tables 4 and Figures 2-6) involves no human participants - its "re-annotation" curves assume an oracle re-annotator - so it is not coded as an experiment. The paper's human-subject work is two separate Prolific studies ("We launched two studies in Prolific, one for natural language inference task (SNLI dataset) and one for stance detection task (SemEval2016 dataset)", Section 5.1.4); each has its own participant sample and its own task, so each is coded as a separate experiment.

**Design.** Mixed design (Section 5.1.2): verifier type (random / baseline / ours) x score quantile (bottom 1st-100th / 101st-200th / 201st-300th) = 9 cells between subjects, 30 participants each = 270 analysed participants; LLM assistance (No LLM assistance / LLM label / LLM label & explanation) within subjects. The human-alone vs. human-AI contrast is the within-subjects assistance factor, hence Exp_Design = "Mixed, Within-Subjects" and Comp_Type = "Dependent Samples"; N_Human = N_HumanAI = 270.

**Reference arms.** The human-alone arm is the "No LLM assistance" phase of the same 270 participants; its value is shared by both assistance conditions. The AI-alone value for the individual-annotator accuracy rows is NOT reported: the paper never states GPT-3.5's accuracy on the verifier-selected instances the participants actually saw (Section 6.2 only notes that observed LLM accuracy ranged from ">80%" to "<30%" across between-subject cells). GPT-3.5's whole-sample accuracy (Table 5, "#anno = 0 / LLM" column) refers to a different item population and was deliberately NOT copied into those rows. Table 1 (page 3) quotes human accuracy for these benchmarks from prior literature (SNLI 0.97 [23], SemEval 0.82 [33]); those are other papers' expert/original annotators, not this study's participants, and are not used.

**Condition structure.** Two kinds of human-AI arm are recorded. (a) The two within-subject LLM-assistance treatments (conditions 1-2), for which individual-annotator accuracy and annotation time are reported. (b) The three end-to-end pipeline arms of Table 5 (conditions 3-5), in which GPT-3.5 labels the whole dataset, a selection rule (random / baseline verifier / our random-forest verifier) picks the bottom-ranked instances, and crowd workers re-annotate them. For (b) the three re-annotation budgets (bottom 100 / 200 / 300 instances) are coded as three measure rows inside each verifier condition rather than as separate conditions; a coder who prefers one condition per arm can split each into three. Table 5 pools the three LLM-assistance treatments (three crowd workers per treatment per instance, majority-voted), so AI_Expl_Incl / Interaction_Mode for conditions 3-5 describe the framework rather than a pure arm - their condition confidence is set to low for this reason.

**Figures.** Figures 8, 9, 13, 14 and 15 are box plots that print only significance stars, no values; only numbers quoted in the running text were extracted. Figure 9 (accuracy split by whether the LLM label was correct) and Figure 13 (accuracy by verifier type) therefore contribute no measure rows. No SDs are reported anywhere for the human or human-AI arms.

**Other.** Attention-check pass rates were 78.95% (NLI study) and 88.82% (stance study); only participants who passed are in the 270. The appendix referenced throughout (demographics, interface screenshots, verifier ablations) is not contained in this 21-page PDF, and pdfdetach reports no embedded files.

**This experiment.** Natural language inference on SNLI: premise/hypothesis pairs labelled entailment, neutral or contradiction, scored against the dataset's gold labels. Individual-annotator accuracy is reported in the text for all three assistance treatments (70.44% / 72.07% / 74.15%). Annotation time for SNLI is plotted (Figure 14) but no values are printed and the text reports only that there was no statistically significant difference between the no-assistance and LLM-label treatments.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Scope of this record.** Section 4 of the paper (verifier benchmarking on six text-classification datasets, Tables 4 and Figures 2-6) involves no human participants - its "re-annotation" curves assume an oracle re-annotator - so it is not coded as an experiment. The paper's human-subject work is two separate Prolific studies ("We launched two studies in Prolific, one for natural language inference task (SNLI dataset) and one for stance detection task (SemEval2016 dataset)", Section 5.1.4); each has its own participant sample and its own task, so each is coded as a separate experiment.

**Design.** Mixed design (Section 5.1.2): verifier type (random / baseline / ours) x score quantile (bottom 1st-100th / 101st-200th / 201st-300th) = 9 cells between subjects, 30 participants each = 270 analysed participants; LLM assistance (No LLM assistance / LLM label / LLM label & explanation) within subjects. The human-alone vs. human-AI contrast is the within-subjects assistance factor, hence Exp_Design = "Mixed, Within-Subjects" and Comp_Type = "Dependent Samples"; N_Human = N_HumanAI = 270.

**Reference arms.** The human-alone arm is the "No LLM assistance" phase of the same 270 participants; its value is shared by both assistance conditions. The AI-alone value for the individual-annotator accuracy rows is NOT reported: the paper never states GPT-3.5's accuracy on the verifier-selected instances the participants actually saw (Section 6.2 only notes that observed LLM accuracy ranged from ">80%" to "<30%" across between-subject cells). GPT-3.5's whole-sample accuracy (Table 5, "#anno = 0 / LLM" column) refers to a different item population and was deliberately NOT copied into those rows. Table 1 (page 3) quotes human accuracy for these benchmarks from prior literature (SNLI 0.97 [23], SemEval 0.82 [33]); those are other papers' expert/original annotators, not this study's participants, and are not used.

**Condition structure.** Two kinds of human-AI arm are recorded. (a) The two within-subject LLM-assistance treatments (conditions 1-2), for which individual-annotator accuracy and annotation time are reported. (b) The three end-to-end pipeline arms of Table 5 (conditions 3-5), in which GPT-3.5 labels the whole dataset, a selection rule (random / baseline verifier / our random-forest verifier) picks the bottom-ranked instances, and crowd workers re-annotate them. For (b) the three re-annotation budgets (bottom 100 / 200 / 300 instances) are coded as three measure rows inside each verifier condition rather than as separate conditions; a coder who prefers one condition per arm can split each into three. Table 5 pools the three LLM-assistance treatments (three crowd workers per treatment per instance, majority-voted), so AI_Expl_Incl / Interaction_Mode for conditions 3-5 describe the framework rather than a pure arm - their condition confidence is set to low for this reason.

**Figures.** Figures 8, 9, 13, 14 and 15 are box plots that print only significance stars, no values; only numbers quoted in the running text were extracted. Figure 9 (accuracy split by whether the LLM label was correct) and Figure 13 (accuracy by verifier type) therefore contribute no measure rows. No SDs are reported anywhere for the human or human-AI arms.

**Other.** Attention-check pass rates were 78.95% (NLI study) and 88.82% (stance study); only participants who passed are in the 270. The appendix referenced throughout (demographics, interface screenshots, verifier ablations) is not contained in this 21-page PDF, and pdfdetach reports no embedded files.

**This experiment.** Stance detection on SemEval-2016: tweets labelled favor, against or none towards a given target, scored against the dataset's gold labels. Individual-annotator accuracy by assistance treatment is plotted (Figure 8) but NOT reported numerically - the text states only that results "did not show any statistically significant differences between AI assistance treatments" - so the accuracy rows for conditions 1-2 are left null. Annotation time is reported in the text for this dataset (12.06 s with no assistance vs. 13.20 s with the LLM label shown, Mann-Whitney U, Section 5.2.4); 7,461 of 8,100 stance tasks survived the idle/outlier exclusions.

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Study A (RQ1-RQ3).** Within-subjects: for each of 10 SMS messages (5 phishing, 5 legitimate) every participant first answered Q1 with no AI ("Do you think this message is a legitimate message or a fraudulent phishing message?"), and only then could open the SmishX explanation and answer Q2. The **Q1 answers are the human-alone reference arm**, the Q2 answers the human-AI condition - the same 125 people, hence Dependent Samples and N_Human = N_HumanAI = 125.

**AI-alone reference arm is reported in words, not as a number.** The paper never prints an AI-alone accuracy for the 10 study messages. It does state (Sec. 6.4) that the Study B run used "the same 10 messages used in Study A ... (where AI was correct)" and (Sec. 6.3) that "For all the disagreement cases, AI's decisions are always aligned with the ground truth (i.e., AI is correct)". Avg_Perf_AI = 1.000 is therefore derived (Est_ES = true in every row).

**The Section 4 system evaluation is NOT coded as an experiment** - it has no human participants. For context: on a separate 1,200-message dataset SmishX reached 98.8% overall accuracy (100.0% phishing, 99.1% spam, 98.2% legitimate; Table 1, PDF p.7), beating ablations without external context (96.0%) and without spam prompts (89.7%), and beating SpaLLM-Guard (96.8%) and PhishE (85.0%) (Table 2). Appendix A (Table 9, PDF p.17) repeats the pipeline with open-source models: DeepSeek-v3 96.2% overall, Qwen2.5-vl-72b-instruct 87.4%. These numbers are on a different item set and a partly three-way (phishing/spam/legitimate) labelling, so they are deliberately NOT used as the AI-alone values in the measure rows. Section 4.3's explanation-quality ratings (completeness 2.98/3, factual consistency 0.99/1, two coders over 180 messages) are annotators scoring AI output, not a decision experiment.

**Subgroups.** Only the 65+ subgroup (n = 50) is broken out in Table 4; the 18-64 complement is never reported, so PROMPT.md's rule for splitting subgroups into conditions is not met and the 65+ values are carried as a clearly labelled extra measure row that overlaps the "All" row.

**Reported outcomes deliberately excluded from `measures`** (no human/AI/human-AI triple, or not task performance): SUS usability 82.6 mean / 82.5 median (85.3 for older adults); trust in AI 3.496 -> 4.264 and self-confidence 3.376 -> 3.640 on 1-5 scales (Table 7); human-AI disagreement on 90/1,250 assessments (7.2%), 11.5% on legitimate vs. 2.9% on phishing SMS, with 44/125 participants (35.2%) disagreeing at least once; 97/125 (77.6%) never opened the detailed AI report (Table 8); ~60 s system latency; logistic regressions on who improved (Table 5) and who rated usability highly (Table 6).

**No SDs, SEs or CIs are printed for any accuracy**, only paired t statistics, so no SD could be computed for either human arm.

**Task framing.** Participants judged only legitimate vs. phishing (binary); the underlying SmishX system is three-way (phishing / spam / legitimate) but "We do not consider spam messages since they are not the main focus of the study" (Sec. 5.2). URLs were partially masked with "xxxx" for participant safety.

paper_metadata.title: Large language model diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial

experiments.Exp_Notes:
**Design.** Single two-arm parallel-group, single-blind RCT (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06774612). All 60 enrolled physicians first completed the same 20-hour AI-literacy training, then were randomized to GPT-4o plus conventional resources (intervention) or conventional resources only (control). 58 were analysed (29 per arm; 2 withdrew), completing 342 cases (172 LLM, 170 control) in 75 minutes. Graders were blinded to arm; outcomes analysed at case level with mixed-effects models.

**Reference arms.** Human-alone = 'Physicians plus conventional resources'. AI-alone = the secondary exploratory 'LLM alone' arm: a researcher applied one fixed zero-shot prompt, three independent runs per vignette (3 x 6 = 18 observations), graded blind with the same rubric; mean 82.9% (s.d. 10.4%). The AI-alone value is reported only overall, so it is repeated in every condition's score row. No time per case was recorded for the LLM-alone arm, so the AI column of the time rows is null. All three arms (human alone, AI alone, human+AI) are therefore available on the same diagnostic-reasoning-score scale; the task is Decide (graded against expert-validated rubrics).

**Conditions.** Condition 1 is the pre-specified overall comparison. Conditions 2-7 are the pre-specified subgroup analyses of the same trial (years of practice below/above the 8.5-year median, self-reported LLM experience less/more than monthly, male/female), coded as separate conditions because Tables 2 and 3 report both the human-alone and the human-AI value for each subgroup. They are subsets of condition 1 and overlap it and each other - do not pool them with condition 1.

**Missing / not extracted.** Subgroup participant counts are reported only for gender (Table 1); years-of-practice and LLM-experience subgroup Ns are not reported and are left null. The exploratory final-diagnosis accuracy outcome (difference 34.3 pp; 95% CI 29.7 to 38.8) has its arm means only in Supplementary Table 8, which is not included in this PDF, so no measure row was created for it. A pre-planned sensitivity analysis adding incomplete cases gives 28.0 pp (95% CI 23.2 to 32.8) - a re-analysis of the same data, not a separate experiment or row.

**Discrepancies.** (1) The Subgroup-analyses paragraph calls the second LLM-experience subgroup 'those using LLMs monthly or less often' while Tables 2 and 3 label it 'More than monthly' (the Reporting Summary states the categorisation was 'less than monthly or more than monthly usage'); the table labels were used. (2) The body text gives the control time as '635 (289.2)' s, Table 3 as '635.0 (289.2)'; the table value was used. (3) The text reports the below-median-practice effect as '30.0 pp' and Table 2 prints '30'; this is a display difference only and no extracted value depends on it.

**Other.** Participant_Source is recorded as the paper states it ('email distribution lists at the LUMS Learning Institute'); in the codebook vocabulary this is 'Email Lists'. Complementarity result: the LLM alone beat LLM-assisted physicians by 11.5 pp (95% CI 5.5 to 17.5), yet in 31.4% of cases the physician-plus-LLM group exceeded the median LLM-alone performance.
